narrativeReportMd:
# Basic R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Basic is still present in R6 with the same canonical identity, base resource, and local element set. I found no local element removals, renames, moves, cardinality narrowing, or R4-to-R6 hard instance breaks. The material local issues are migration and conformance risks: `Basic.code` has a stronger and different terminology binding, `Basic.created` widened from `date` to `dateTime`, and `Basic.author` can now point to `Device` or `CareTeam`.

## Scope
The report covers Basic's local StructureDefinition and related local terminology artifacts. Inherited Resource and DomainResource differences are out of scope and should be handled by the base-artifact reports.

## Main migration themes
The biggest R4-to-R6 issue is semantic/conformance migration for `Basic.code`: R4's example Basic Resource Types code system is replaced by an extensible binding to current and past FHIR resource type codes. The biggest R6-to-R4 issues are lossless representation: R6 `created` timestamps and R6 `author` references to `Device` or `CareTeam` are not valid under the R4 Basic element definitions.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact reverse-compatibility findings are `Basic.created` accepting dateTime precision and `Basic.author` adding two reference targets. The terminology finding for `Basic.code` is medium impact but requires human review because extensible-binding applicability depends on the intended Basic resource concept.

## Findings requiring human review
`Basic.code` should be reviewed by terminology and migration owners. Some old R4 codes have obvious conceptual relationships to R6 resource type names, but the systems and code values differ and no local ConceptMap was found.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The R6 model changes are mostly additive or widening, so R4-to-R6 structural migration is generally safe. Backward compatibility would have been easier if `Basic.code` had retained the old value set as an additional accepted coding or if an official ConceptMap had been provided.

## Follow-up analysis
Base Resource/DomainResource reports should own inherited snapshot changes. A terminology follow-up should map `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/basic-resource-type` to R6 resource-type codes where appropriate.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: Basic has no local R4-to-R6 hard structural break, but it does have three material migration risks: a stronger/different `Basic.code` binding, `Basic.created` changing from `date` to `dateTime`, and `Basic.author` adding `Device` and `CareTeam` targets. The top uncertainty is how R4 Basic Resource Types codes should map to R6 version-independent resource type codes.
summary.migrationThemesMd: R4 Basic instances should usually parse structurally in R6, but terminology conformance and generated model types need attention. Reverse conversion from R6 to R4 is not lossless when R6 uses time-of-day precision in `created` or the new `author` target types. `Basic.code` migration may require a ConceptMap or profile-specific policy because the code is a modifier and drives interpretation of the whole Basic instance.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for element identity, cardinality, type, reference-target, and binding-strength deltas because they come directly from local StructureDefinition files. Overall confidence is medium because the most nuanced finding, `Basic.code`, depends on extensible-binding applicability and no official diff, narrative rationale, expansion, or ConceptMap was available locally.

findings.title: Basic.code binding changed from example Basic Resource Types to extensible version-independent resource types

oldState.summary: R4 `Basic.code` was a mandatory CodeableConcept with an example binding to `ValueSet/basic-resource-type`.

binding.description: Codes for identifying types of resources not yet defined by FHIR.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R4 ValueSet includes the complete R4 code system `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/basic-resource-type` with lower-case/abbreviated codes such as `consent`, `referral`, `advevent`, `aptmtreq`, `account`, and `invoice`.

flags.isModifierReason: This element determines what kind of resource is being represented which drives the meaning of all of the other elements.

semanticText.definition: Identifies the 'type' of resource - equivalent to the resource name for other resources.
semanticText.comment:
Because resource references will only be able to indicate 'Basic', the type of reference will need to be specified in a Profile identified as part of the resource.  Refer to the resource notes section for information on appropriate terminologies for this code.

semanticText.requirements: Must be able to distinguish different types of Basic resources.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, the binding was only `example`. Validators and conformant implementations could accept other codings without treating them as terminology non-conformance.

newState.summary: R6 `Basic.code` remains a mandatory CodeableConcept but now has an extensible binding to `ValueSet/version-independent-resource-types`.

binding.description: Codes for all resources across R5 and all published previous versions since R2

These use FHIR resource type names such as `Consent`, `AdverseEvent`, `Account`, `Invoice`, and old resource names such as `ReferralRequest`, not the R4 Basic Resource Types code system.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, if a current or past FHIR resource type code applies to the Basic concept, an extensible binding creates a conformance expectation to use a code from the R6 value set.

facts.note: This is a local Basic differential change on the modifier element `Basic.code`.
The old and new value sets use different code systems and different code shapes.

facts.oldValue: Codes for identifying types of resources not yet defined by FHIR.
facts.newValue: Codes for all resources across R5 and all published previous versions since R2

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `Basic.code` has the same id, path, cardinality, type, modifier flag, definition, and requirements in both versions; only the binding strength/value set/description changed materially.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a simple structural parse break because `Basic.code` is still `1..1 CodeableConcept`. The risk is conformance and semantics: R4 instances using the old Basic Resource Types code system can become terminology-nonconformant or receive validator warnings/errors under R6 if the intended concept is covered by the R6 extensible value set. Runtime risk is medium because `code` is a modifier and many implementations branch on it to decide how to interpret the rest of a Basic resource.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misclassifying a Basic resource type can affect routing, display, authorization, and downstream business rules because `Basic.code` determines the meaning of the resource.

justification.inferredGoal: Align Basic.code with stable current and historical FHIR resource type identifiers rather than a draft/example list of provisional Basic resource types.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Broaden the R6 base value set to include the R4 Basic Resource Types codes while recommending version-independent resource-type codings.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of aligning `Basic.code` with current and historical FHIR resource type identifiers is reasonable because `Basic.code` is a modifier that controls interpretation of the resource. A less-breaking base design was possible, but it would keep legacy lower-case Basic Resource Types beside official resource-type codes and weaken the terminology cleanup. Given the uneven overlap and modifier semantics, the breakage is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base alternative would have been to compose the R6 extensible value set from both version-independent resource types and the old R4 Basic Resource Types system, or to retain a weaker base binding while making resource-type codes preferred in guidance. That would preserve old instances with only the old coding. It is only a partial alternative: old abbreviated codes and official resource-type names would both remain valid for the same concept, deprecated representations might never disappear, and validators/consumers would face ambiguity on an element that determines the whole Basic instance meaning. A ConceptMap or dual-coding migration note would help migration but is not itself a backwards-compatible base design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Would preserve many R4 codings, but creates durable duplicate code representations and validation ambiguity for a modifier element.

evidence.detail: R4 binding strength is `example` and valueSet is `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/basic-resource-type`.
R6 binding strength is `extensible` and valueSet is `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/version-independent-resource-types`.
The R4 Basic Resource Types code system contains draft lower-case/abbreviated codes including `consent`, `referral`, `advevent`, and `aptmtreq`.
The R6 value set imports current resource type codes and `http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-old-types`.

examples.examplesMd: The old example is structurally valid Basic content and illustrates the terminology risk. Whether it is formally invalid, a warning, or acceptable as an alternate coding in R6 depends on validator policy and whether the concept is judged to be covered by the extensible R6 value set.

findings.narrativeMd: `Basic.code` is the most semantically important Basic-local element because it is marked as a modifier and identifies what kind of resource the Basic instance represents. R4 gave only an example binding to a draft Basic Resource Types code system. R6 replaces that with an extensible binding to current and historical FHIR resource type codes. Existing R4 instances that used the old example codes may need explicit terminology migration rather than a purely structural version bump.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No JSON property was removed and the datatype remains `CodeableConcept`, so this is not a universal R4-valid/R6-invalid structural break. The validation mechanism is terminology binding strength: R6 extensible binding can make an old coding non-conformant when a suitable R6 resource-type code exists. In the R6-to-R4 direction, R4 can still carry arbitrary CodeableConcept codings, but R4 consumers that switch on the old example code system may not understand R6 resource-type codes.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory `Basic.code` codings before migration. Where an old Basic Resource Types code corresponds to a current or past FHIR resource, map to the R6 resource-type code and consider whether the Basic instance should instead be transformed to the actual resource. Where no R6 resource-type code applies, preserve the local coding and document why the extensible value set does not cover the concept. Add tests for old-only coding, dual coding, and R6-only coding.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is probably justified as terminology cleanup, but it is only partially backward-compatible. A published ConceptMap or a transitional dual-coding recommendation would have allowed R4 data to migrate with less local interpretation while still encouraging R6 resource-type codes.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is needed because the key question for extensible bindings is not simply membership but applicability: if an R6 resource type accurately represents the Basic concept, R6 expects that code; if not, alternate codings can be justified.

findings.title: Basic.created widened from date to dateTime

semanticText.definition: Identifies when the resource was first created.
semanticText.requirements: Allows ordering resource instances by time.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could capture the creation date but not a time-of-day on this element.

semanticText.definition: Identifies when the resource was first created.
semanticText.requirements: Allows ordering resource instances by time.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can capture date-only values and more precise timestamps, including time-of-day and timezone.

facts.note: The cardinality and semantic text are otherwise unchanged.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `Basic.created` has the same id/path, cardinality, flags, definition, and requirements in both versions; the primitive type changed from `date` to `dateTime`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a widening for R4-to-R6: normal FHIR date lexical values are also valid at date precision for `dateTime`, so existing R4 values should remain representable. It is a direct reverse-compatibility break when R6 uses time precision because R4 `date` cannot carry a time or timezone. Generated models may also change the property type from date-only to date-time, affecting serializers, database columns, and equality/order logic.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily ordering, audit, and business-process precision rather than direct clinical safety.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow Basic creation time to be represented with the same precision often needed for ordering and audit-like use cases.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not an R4-to-R6 base-design break: R4 date values remain valid at date precision for R6 dateTime.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing dateTime precision directly supports the existing ordering and audit-like requirement and does not invalidate R4 date-only instances in R6. The only material incompatibility is reverse conversion when R6 uses time-of-day precision, so the change is probably justified under the calibration rules.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible base R6 alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility because the R6 type widening preserves R4 instances. Keeping `created` as `date` and adding an extension for time precision would be an R6-to-R4 downgrade-friendly design, but that is a mitigation/backport strategy rather than a less-breaking answer to an R4-to-R6 base-design break.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is only for R6-to-R4 downgrade; preserving full timestamps in R4 would require truncation or an extension/backport mitigation.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example truncates a timestamp to a date. That is structurally R4-compatible but loses time-of-day and timezone information.

findings.narrativeMd: `Basic.created` changed from `date` to `dateTime`. For R4-to-R6 migration this is a widening and should not invalidate existing date-only values. The practical break is reverse conversion and generated code: R6 instances may contain timestamps that R4 validators and R4 date-only model properties cannot accept without truncation or an extension.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `created: "2026-05-17"` remains compatible with R6 `dateTime` precision. An R6 instance with `created: "2026-05-17T21:45:00+02:00"` is not valid for R4 `date`. Strict R4 parsers, JSON schemas, database constraints, and generated model setters typed as date-only can reject the R6 value.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, update generated models and tests to expect a dateTime-capable field. For R6-to-R4, decide whether to truncate to the calendar date, preserve the original timestamp in an extension, or reject records where time precision matters. Test date-only, partial-date, and full timestamp inputs.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been made reverse-compatible by leaving `created` as `date` and adding a separate optional precise timestamp extension. That would avoid R4 downgrade loss but would keep a less precise base field for an element used for ordering.

findings.title: Basic.author added Device and CareTeam reference targets

oldState.summary: R4 `Basic.author` allowed Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, RelatedPerson, and Organization.

semanticText.definition: Indicates who was responsible for creating the resource instance.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 limited authorship to people, roles, patients/related persons, and organizations.

newState.summary: R6 `Basic.author` also allows Device and CareTeam.

semanticText.definition: Indicates who was responsible for creating the resource instance.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 recognizes that a Basic resource can be authored by a device or by a care team as a collective actor.

facts.note: `Device` and `CareTeam` are new allowed targets in R6.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `Basic.author` has the same id/path, cardinality, type code, flags, definition, and requirements; only the Reference targetProfile list widened.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Adding reference targets is non-breaking for R4-to-R6 validation because all R4 targets are still allowed. It is a hard reverse-validation problem: an R6 Basic whose author is a `Device` or `CareTeam` is outside R4's targetProfile list for `Basic.author`. Generated clients may also need enum, type-union, switch, authorization, or resolver updates for the additional target types.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The likely risk is attribution or workflow misrouting if a system assumes every author is a human/organization actor. Direct clinical safety risk was not identified from the StructureDefinition alone.

justification.inferredGoal: Support device-generated and team-authored Basic resources without requiring profiles or extensions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not an R4-to-R6 base-design break: R6 adds Device and CareTeam targets while preserving every R4 author target.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting device-generated and team-authored Basic resources fits the existing authorship definition and preserves all R4-valid author references. The incompatibility arises only when converting newer R6 content with Device or CareTeam authors back to R4, so the base R6 widening is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible base R6 alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility because all R4 target profiles remain valid. Keeping the R4 target list and representing Device or CareTeam authorship through Provenance, extensions, or profile-specific rules would be a downgrade-friendly mitigation, not a less-breaking base-design alternative for existing R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: There is no R4-to-R6 compatibility tradeoff; R6-to-R4 downgrade of new targets needs mapping, rejection, Provenance, or extension handling.

evidence.detail: R4 targetProfile list contains Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Patient, RelatedPerson, and Organization.
R6 targetProfile list adds Device and CareTeam.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example uses an illustrative extension URL only. A real downgrade should use an agreed cross-version extension or profile-specific mapping.

findings.narrativeMd: `Basic.author` now permits two additional target types. This is a widening in R6 and does not break old R4 instances. The practical break appears when an R6 Basic uses one of the new targets and must be validated, stored, or transformed as R4.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation remains compatible for existing author references because all R4 target profiles are preserved. R6-to-R4 validation fails or becomes profile-nonconformant if `author.reference` resolves to `Device` or `CareTeam`. Some generated R4 clients may not reject the raw reference string immediately, but conformance-aware validators, resolvers, and typed APIs will treat the target as outside the R4 domain.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, identify `author` references to `Device` or `CareTeam`. If the target can be represented by an Organization, Practitioner, or PractitionerRole without changing meaning, map it explicitly and preserve the original reference in an extension or Provenance. Otherwise, reject downgrade or require profile-specific handling. Add tests for each allowed author target.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is a reasonable expressiveness improvement but not losslessly backward-compatible. The less-breaking approach would have used Provenance or extensions for device/team authorship, at the cost of making common attribution harder to discover in the base Basic resource.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Basic remains present in R6 with the same canonical URL, id, name, kind `resource`, type `Basic`, abstract flag `false`, derivation `specialization`, and baseDefinition `DomainResource`. Maturity/status changes are noted as non-breaking.
The local Basic element set is unchanged: `identifier`, `code`, `subject`, `created`, and `author`. No local element was removed, added, renamed, split, merged, or moved.
All local Basic element cardinalities are unchanged: `identifier` remains `0..*`, `code` remains `1..1`, `subject` remains `0..1`, `created` remains `0..1`, and `author` remains `0..1`.

No Basic-specific local invariant was added, removed, or changed in the Basic differential. Snapshot constraint differences observed on inherited elements and root DomainResource constraints are out of scope for this Basic report.
No local Basic element has a fixed value, pattern, or default value in either R4 or R6.
No local Basic element introduced or removed maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue constraints.
`Basic.code` remains the only local modifier element and keeps the same modifier reason. Other local Basic elements remain non-modifier.
Local summary flags are unchanged: `identifier`, `code`, `subject`, `created`, and `author` remain summary elements. Inherited summary flag changes, if any, are out of scope.
No local Basic element has slicing in either version.
Local element definitions, short text, comments, and requirements are materially stable. Binding descriptions changed for `Basic.code` and are covered in the terminology finding.

No local element names, JSON property names, choice suffixes, or containment shape changed. Serialization risk is limited to the reported primitive type change for `created` and the reported reference target expansion for `author`.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Basic maturity advanced from draft/trial-use FMM 1 to active/normative FMM 3
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The canonical identity, kind, type, abstract flag, and baseDefinition did not change. Maturity/status metadata changes do not by themselves invalidate instances or change JSON serialization.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance or dependency policies that treat normative/active artifacts differently may need metadata updates, but instance migration is not required for this metadata change alone.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited snapshot differences are visible in Basic, including Resource/DomainResource constraint text, Resource.language binding, contained-resource wording, and inherited summary/modifier-extension behavior. Per assignment, those should be assessed in the base artifact reports, not duplicated here.

A ConceptMap or official migration note would materially improve migration of R4 `Basic.code` values such as `consent`, `referral`, `advevent`, and `aptmtreq` to R6 resource type codes where appropriate.

The `Basic.created` finding relies on normal FHIR primitive lexical compatibility between date precision and dateTime precision. Any separate datatype-level breaking change should be handled in the datatype reports.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The analysis used local package artifacts and did not include an official R4-to-R6 diff, Jira issue trail, or ballot reconciliation notes for Basic.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Provide official change notes or a generated official diff for Basic.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The `Basic.code` terminology finding compares local ValueSet composition and CodeSystem content, not a terminology-server expansion or an official applicability analysis for the extensible binding.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run R4 and R6 expansions with the intended terminology server and obtain or author a ConceptMap from the R4 Basic Resource Types code system to R6 resource-type codes.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No implementation usage data or Basic examples were found in the core packages, so prevalence estimates for old `Basic.code` values, timestamped `created`, and new `author` targets are judgment calls.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Analyze real R4/R6 Basic instances or implementation guide profiles that constrain Basic.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The new artifact is an R6 ballot build (`6.0.0-ballot4`), not a final normative R6 release. Findings could change before publication.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Re-run the comparison against the final published R6 core package.
